## Overview

Mixing up the layout of conditional probability tables is the most common bug in Bayesian
network software. Every file format flattens a table to a list of numbers, and the formats
do not agree on the order. This vignette walks through the reference ecological network of
SPEC section 45 (`Climate → SoilMoisture ← Irrigation`, `SoilMoisture → Vegetation ←
GrazingPressure`, `Vegetation → HabitatQuality → Occupancy`) in every format and shows how
each file's numbers become the same Julia array.

The IR convention (ADR 0002) is: for `P(Y | X1, ..., Xk)` the table has
`size == (n(X1), ..., n(Xk), n(Y))`, parents in the order they are listed in the file, and it
is normalised over the last axis.

## Setup

The reference network is a fixture in all six formats, so one `read_network` per format
gives six IRs to compare.

```{julia}
using BayesianNetworkFormats

files = ["dne/habitat_reference.dne", "xdsl/habitat_reference.xdsl", "net/habitat_reference.net",
         "bif/habitat_reference.bif", "dsc/habitat_reference.dsc", "uai/habitat_reference.uai"]
habitat = Dict(f => read_network(fixture_path(f)) for f in files)
sm = variable(habitat["dne/habitat_reference.dne"], :SoilMoisture)
sm.parents, sm.states, size(sm.table)
```

A helper prints the lines of a fixture that belong to one node:

```{julia}
function show_block(name, pattern, n)
    lines = readlines(fixture_path(name))
    i = findfirst(l -> occursin(pattern, l), lines)
    println(join(lines[i:min(i + n - 1, length(lines))], "\n"))
end
```

## Row-major with the child fastest: Netica, GeNIe, HUGIN, UAI

Netica [@NeticaFileFormats], GeNIe [@GeNIeDocs], HUGIN [@HuginNET] and UAI [@UAIFormat] all
write the table row-major over `(parents..., child)`: the child's state changes fastest, then
the last parent, and the first parent slowest.

The `habitat_reference.*` fixtures used in this section were written by this package, so
they show *our rendering* of the convention rather than evidence for it; the row comments
are ours too. The evidence is at the end of the section: files written by Netica, GeNIe and
a third-party UAI tool that only normalise when read this way.

```{julia}
show_block("dne/habitat_reference.dne", "node SoilMoisture", 16)
```

Modern Netica nests one pair of parentheses per parent; old Netica writes the same numbers as
one flat list. Both are read by collecting the numbers and ignoring the nesting:

```{julia}
show_block("dne/habitat_reference_flat.dne", "node SoilMoisture", 16)
```

The same sequence goes inside GeNIe's `<probabilities>`:

```{julia}
show_block("xdsl/habitat_reference.xdsl", "<cpt id=\"SoilMoisture\">", 7)
```

HUGIN nests parentheses like Netica (the `%` comments are written by this package):

```{julia}
show_block("net/habitat_reference.net", "potential (SoilMoisture", 10)
```

UAI lists the scope of each function with the child last and then the numbers with the
last scope variable fastest [@UAIFormat]:

```{julia}
lines = readlines(fixture_path("uai/habitat_reference.uai"))
println(join(lines[1:12], "\n"))
println("...")
i = findfirst(==("18"), lines)
println(join(lines[i:(i + 6)], "\n"))
```

### Files written by the tools themselves

Two fixtures in this package were written elsewhere. `xdsl/Habitat_Suitability.xdsl` is
record 132 of the Bayesian Network Model Archive [@BNMA], written by GeNIe 2.0 [@GeNIeDocs];
`PreyNumbers` has one three-state row per terrain type, and only the child-fastest reading
gives rows that sum to one:

```{julia}
show_block("xdsl/Habitat_Suitability.xdsl", "<cpt id=\"PreyNumbers\">", 7)
```

```{julia}
tiger = read_network(fixture_path("xdsl/Habitat_Suitability.xdsl"))
prey = variable(tiger, :PreyNumbers)
prey.parents, prey.table[1, :], sum(prey.table; dims=2)[:, 1]
```

`uai/ChestClinic.uai` is the *asia* network [@LauritzenSpiegelhalter1988] in UAI `BAYES`
form [@UAIFormat], written by the Merlin library. Read with the last scope variable as the
child and the child fastest, it reproduces the published marginal `P(dysp = yes) = 0.436`, a
number this package had no hand in:

```{julia}
chest = read_network(fixture_path("uai/ChestClinic.uai"))
variable(chest, :X7).parents, round.(marginal(chest, :X7); digits=5)
```

Both files are recorded with their origin and licence in `test/fixtures/LICENSES.md`. The
Netica-written BNMA models [@BNMA; @Kotalik2026] in `EcologicalBayesianNetworks.jl/models/`
play the same role for `.dne`: the test suite reads them, with their `#k` findings and
`levels` [@NeticaFileFormats], whenever the sibling checkout is present.

### `from_rowmajor`

All four are converted with one function. Given the flat list and the dimensions
`(n(p1), ..., n(pk), n(child))`, `from_rowmajor` reshapes with the dimensions reversed (so
that Julia's column-major order matches the file's row-major order) and then reverses the
axes back:

```{julia}
vals = [0.7, 0.25, 0.05, 0.3, 0.5, 0.2, 0.3, 0.5, 0.2, 0.1, 0.4, 0.5, 0.1, 0.4, 0.5, 0.05, 0.25, 0.7]
t = from_rowmajor(vals, (3, 2, 3))
t == sm.table
```

```{julia}
t[1, 2, :]   # Climate = dry, Irrigation = high
```

A plain `reshape` would silently give a different table whose rows do not sum to one:

```{julia}
wrong = reshape(vals, 3, 2, 3)
wrong[1, 2, :], sum(wrong[1, 2, :])
```

`to_rowmajor` is the inverse and is what every writer uses:

```{julia}
to_rowmajor(sm.table) == vals
```

## BIF: rows in any order, or `table` with the child slowest

The bnlearn dialect of BIF [@Cozman1998; @Scutari2010] gives one row per parent
configuration, labelled with the parent states in parent order. Rows may appear in any
order, so the reader indexes them by state name rather than position (bnlearn happens to
write the first parent fastest):

```{julia}
show_block("bif/habitat_reference.bif", "probability ( SoilMoisture", 8)
```

pgmpy and the original BIF specification [@Cozman1998] use a `table` line instead. Its
numbers are in *header* order, `(child, parent1, ..., parentk)`, with the last variable
fastest, so the child is now the slowest index. The reader reshapes with `from_rowmajor` over
`(n(child), n(p1), ..., n(pk))` and then moves the child axis to the end:

```{julia}
show_block("bif/sprinkler_table.bif", "probability ( Grass", 3)
```

```{julia}
grass = variable(read_network(fixture_path("bif/sprinkler_table.bif")), :Grass)
grass.parents, grass.table[1, 1, :], grass.table[2, 2, :]   # (on, yes) and (off, no)
```

## DSC: 0-based indices in parent order

DSC rows [@Kadie2001] carry 0-based state indices instead of names, again in parent order
and in any order:

```{julia}
show_block("dsc/habitat_reference.dsc", "probability ( SoilMoisture", 8)
```

## One model, six files

After conversion the six IRs agree entry for entry, and the brute-force joint distribution
gives the same marginals from each:

```{julia}
ref = habitat["dne/habitat_reference.dne"]
for f in files
    same = isequivalent(habitat[f], ref; titles=false, positions=false, comments=false, extras=false)
    println(rpad(f, 32), same ? "equivalent   " : "DIFFERENT    ", round.(marginal(habitat[f], :Occupancy); digits=6))
end
```

The direction of the check matters: `SoilMoisture` has parents of different sizes
(`Climate` has three states, `Irrigation` two), so swapping the parent axes changes the shape
and is caught by `validate`. Two parents with the same number of states would not be caught
by shape alone; the cross-format equality tests and the brute-force marginal of *asia*
(`P(dysp = yes) = 0.4360`) [@LauritzenSpiegelhalter1988] in the test suite pin the convention
for that case.

## Summary

Netica, GeNIe, HUGIN and UAI flatten a table row-major over `(parents..., child)` with the
child fastest, so `from_rowmajor` and `to_rowmajor` are the only conversion the package
needs; BIF `table` lines put the child slowest, and BIF and DSC rows are labelled rather than
positional. Tool-written files pin the convention independently: only the child-fastest
reading normalises `Habitat_Suitability.xdsl`, and only it reproduces the published *asia*
marginal from `ChestClinic.uai`. The next vignette, *Influence diagram files*, adds decision
and utility nodes, whose tables follow the same convention over their parents.
